Perhaps some day we shall know how to heighten creativity. Until then, one of the best things we can do for creative men and women is to stand out of their light."]{.f5 .f4-m .f3-l .lh-copy .measure .mt0} [--- John W. Gardner, author and educator (8 Oct 1912-2002)]{.f6 .ttu .tracked .fs-normal} ::: :::: ## {{< iconify noto-v1 package >}} Setting up R Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) # Data Processing in R library(mosaic) # Our workhorse for stats, sampling library(janitor) # Data Cleaning library(skimr) # Good to Examine data library(ggformula) # Formula interface for graphs # load the NHANES data library library(NHANES) library(infer) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: #### Plot Fonts and Theme ::: {.cell messages='false'} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} library(systemfonts) library(showtext) ## Clean the slate systemfonts::clear_local_fonts() systemfonts::clear_registry() ## showtext_opts(dpi = 96) # set DPI for showtext sysfonts::font_add( family = "Alegreya", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Regular.ttf", bold = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Bold.ttf", italic = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Italic.ttf", bolditalic = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-BoldItalic.ttf" ) sysfonts::font_add( family = "Roboto Condensed", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Regular.ttf", bold = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Bold.ttf", italic = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Italic.ttf", bolditalic = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-BoldItalic.ttf" ) showtext_auto(enable = TRUE) # enable showtext ## theme_custom <- function() { theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme( panel.widths = unit(11, "cm"), panel.heights = unit(6.79, "cm") ) + # Golden Ratio theme( plot.margin = margin_auto(t = 1, r = 2, b = 1, l = 1, unit = "cm"), plot.background = element_rect( fill = "bisque", colour = "black", linewidth = 1 ) ) + theme_sub_axis( title = element_text( family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 10 ), text = element_text( family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 8 ) ) + theme_sub_legend( text = element_text( family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 6 ), title = element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 8 ) ) + theme_sub_plot( title = element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 14, face = "bold" ), title.position = "plot", subtitle = element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 10 ), caption = element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 6 ), caption.position = "plot" ) } ## Use available fonts in ggplot text geoms too! ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" )) ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" )) ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "marquee", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" )) ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text_repel", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" )) ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label_repel", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" )) ## Set the theme ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) ## tinytable options options("tinytable_tt_digits" = 2) options("tinytable_format_num_fmt" = "significant_cell") options(tinytable_html_mathjax = TRUE) ## Set defaults for flextable flextable::set_flextable_defaults(font.family = "Roboto Condensed") ``` ::: ## {{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} What is a Population? A *population* is a collection of individuals or observations we are interested in. This is also commonly denoted as a study population in science research, or a *target audience* in design. We mathematically denote the population's size using upper-case `N`. A *population parameter* is some numerical summary about the population that is unknown but you wish you knew. For example, when this quantity is a mean like *the mean height of all Bangaloreans*, the population parameter of interest is the *population mean* $\mu$. A *census* is an exhaustive enumeration or counting of all N individuals in the population. We do this in order to compute the population parameter's value exactly. Of note is that as the number N of individuals in our population increases, conducting a census gets more expensive (in terms of time, energy, and money). ::: callout-important ## {{< iconify carbon parameter >}} Parameters Populations *P*arameters are usually indicated by Greek Letters. ::: ## {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} What is a Sample? Sampling is the act of collecting a small subset from the population, which we generally do when we can't perform a **census**. We mathematically denote the sample size using lower case `n`, as opposed to upper case `N` which denotes the population's size. Typically the sample size `n` is much smaller than the population size `N`. Thus sampling is a much cheaper alternative than performing a census. A **sample statistic**, also known as a *point estimate*, is a summary statistic like a `mean` or `standard deviation` that is computed from a sample. ::: callout-note ## Why do we sample? Because we cannot conduct a census ( not always ) --- and **sometimes we won't even know how big the population is** --- we take samples. And we *still* want to do useful work for/with the population, after estimating its parameters, *an act of generalizing* from sample to population. So the question is, **can we estimate useful parameters of the population, using just samples? Can point estimates serve as useful guides to population parameters?** [This act of generalizing from sample to population is at the heart of **statistical inference**.]{style="background-color: yellow;"} ::: ::: callout-important ## An Alliterative Mnemonic NOTE: there is an [*alliterative*](https://www.grammarly.com/blog/alliteration/) [*mnemonic*](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/mnemonic) here: **S**amples have **S**tatistics; **P**opulations have **P**arameters. ::: ## {{< iconify fluent-mdl2 test-parameter >}} Population Parameters and Sample Statistics | | Population Parameter | Sample Statistic | |--------------------|----------------------|------------------| | Mean | $\mu$ | $\bar{x}$ | | Standard Deviation | $\sigma$ | s | | Proportion | p | $\hat{p}$ | | Correlation | $\rho$ | r | | Slope (Regression) | $\beta_1$ | $b_1$ | : Parameters and Statistics ::: callout-note ## Question Q.1. What is the mean commute time for workers in a particular city? A.1. The *parameter* is the mean commute time $\mu$ for a *population* containing all workers who work in the city. We *estimate* it using $\bar{x}$, the mean of the random sample of people who work in the city. ::: ::: callout-note ## Question Q.2. What is the correlation between the size of dinner bills and the size of tips at a restaurant? A.2. The *parameter is* $\rho$ , the correlation between bill amount and tip size for a *population* of all dinner bills at that restaurant. We estimate it using r, the correlation from a random sample of dinner bills. ::: ::: callout-note ## Question Q.3. How much difference is there in the proportion of 30 to 39-year-old residents who have only a cell phone (no land line phone) compared to 50 to 59-year-olds in the country? A.3. The *population* is all citizens of the country, and the parameter is $p_1 - p_2$, the difference in proportion of 30 to 39-year-old residents who have only a cell phone ($p_1$) and the proportion with the same property among all 50 to 59-year olds ($p_2$). We estimate it using ($\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2}$), the difference in sample proportions computed from random samples taken from each group. ::: Sample statistics vary and in the following we will estimate this uncertainty and decide how reliable they might be as estimates of population parameters. ## {{< iconify mdi head-thinking-outline >}} {{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} So What do We Want? Let us define the purpose we have in mind: - We want to estimate the population parameters, such as the population mean $\mu$ and the population standard deviation $\sigma$. - We want to take ***just one sample*** from the population, and compute the sample statistics such as the sample mean $\bar{x}$ and the sample standard deviation $s$. - (Because that is all we can afford, let us say). - We want to be sure that estimates from the sample are not very much off from the population parameters. - And we want to know how to quantify that uncertainty. To achieve this purpose, we need a certain amount of theoretical justification. Let us now dig into those systematically. ## {{< iconify mdi head-thinking-outline >}} {{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} An "Assumed" Population First something counter-intuitive: we need to *define a population* for the sake of reference. We will use the `NHANES` dataset, and pick one variable out it it, `Height`, and treat it as our population. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data("NHANES") ``` ::: Let us create a NHANES (sub)-dataset without duplicated IDs and only adults and select the `Height` variable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} NHANES_adult <- NHANES %>% distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% filter(Age >= 18) %>% select(Height) %>% drop_na(Height) NHANES_adult %>% glimpse() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 4,790 Columns: 1 $ Height 164.7, 168.4, 166.7, 169.5, 181.9, 169.4, 148.1, 177.8, 181.3, … ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-important ## An "Assumed" Population We will now onwards **treat** this single-variable dataset as our **Population**. So this is our *population*, with appropriate *population parameters* such as `pop_mean`, and `pop_sd`. ::: Let us calculate the **population parameters** for the `Height` data from our "assumed" population: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # NHANES_adult is assumed population pop_mean <- mosaic::mean(~Height, data = NHANES_adult) pop_sd <- mosaic::sd(~Height, data = NHANES_adult) pop_mean ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 168.3497 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pop_sd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.15705 ``` ::: ::: Let us now start our sampling game! ### {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} Sampling Now, we will sample **ONCE** from the `Height` variable. Let us take a sample of `sample size` 50. We will compare **sample statistics** with **population parameters** on the basis of this ONE sample of 50: :::: {layout="[ 40, 60 ]"} ::: {#first-column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(12345) # for reproducibility sample_50 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 50) %>% select(Height) sample_50 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} sample_mean_50 <- mean(~Height, data = sample_50) sample_mean_50 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 170.094 ``` ::: ::: A Single Sample of size 50. ::: ::: {#second-column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Plotting the histogram of this sample ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) sample_50 %>% gf_histogram(~Height, bins = 10) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = ~sample_mean_50, color = "purple" ) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = ~pop_mean, colour = "black" ) %>% gf_annotate("label", y = 7, x = pop_mean - 8, label = "Population Mean", color = "black" ) %>% gf_annotate("label", y = 7, x = sample_mean_50 + 8, label = "Sample Mean", color = "purple" ) %>% gf_annotate("curve", x = sample_mean_50 + 8, y = 6.5, xend = sample_mean_50 + 1, yend = 2, curvature = -0.2, color = "purple", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")) ) %>% gf_annotate("curve", x = pop_mean - 8, y = 6.5, xend = pop_mean - 1, yend = 2, curvature = 0.2, color = "black", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")) ) %>% gf_labs( y = "Frequency", title = "Distribution and Mean of a Single Sample", subtitle = "Sample Size = 50" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Distribution and Mean of a Single Sample](index_files/figure-html/fig-single-sample-1.png){#fig-single-sample width=2100} ::: ::: ::: :::: ### {{< iconify ic baseline-loop >}} {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} {{< iconify icon-park-outline average >}} Repeated Samples and Sample Means OK, so the `sample_mean_50` is not too far from the `pop_mean`. Is this ***always*** true, i.e. for ***any sample***? Let us check: we will create 500 repeated samples, each of size 50. And calculate their mean as the *sample statistic*, giving us a data frame containing 500 `sample means`. We will then see if ***all these 500 means*** lie close to the `pop_mean`: ::: {.cell layout="[75,25]"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} sample_50_500 <- do(500) * { sample(NHANES_adult, size = 50) %>% select(Height) %>% # drop sampling related column "orig.id" summarise( sample_mean = mean(Height), sample_sd = sd(Height), sample_min = min(Height), sample_max = max(Height) ) } sample_50_500 <- sample_50_500 %>% select(.index, sample_mean, sample_sd, sample_min, sample_max) sample_50_500 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} dim(sample_50_500) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 500 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#fig-sample-means-sds .cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) sample_50_500 %>% gf_point(.index ~ sample_mean, color = "purple", title = "Sample Means are close to the Population Mean", subtitle = "Sample Means are Random!", caption = "Grey lines represent our 500 samples" ) %>% gf_segment( .index + .index ~ sample_min + sample_max, color = "grey", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.3, ylab = "Sample Index (1-500)", xlab = "Sample Means" ) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = ~pop_mean, color = "black" ) %>% gf_annotate("label", y = -25, x = pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "black" ) ## sample_50_500 %>% gf_point(.index ~ sample_sd, color = "purple", title = "Sample SDs are close to the Population SD", subtitle = "Sample SDs are Random!", ) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = ~pop_sd, color = "black" ) %>% gf_annotate("label", y = -25, x = pop_sd, label = "Population SD", color = "black" ) %>% gf_refine(lims(x = c(4, 16))) %>% gf_labs(x = "Sample SDs", y = "Sample Index (1-500)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample Means](index_files/figure-html/fig-sample-means-sds-1.png){#fig-sample-means-sds-1 width=2100} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample SDs](index_files/figure-html/fig-sample-means-sds-2.png){#fig-sample-means-sds-2 width=2100} ::: Sample Means and SDs ::: ::: callout-note ### Sample Means and Sample SDs are a Random Variables!![^8] The `sample_mean`s (purple dots @fig-sample-means-sds-1) are all generally in the vicinity of the `pop_mean` (vertical black line). And since they are themselves random [because the samples are random]{.black .bg-gold}, they will have their own distribution, with a`mean` and `sd` too ,over all the 500 sample-means. And the `sample_sd`s are also random (see @fig-sample-means-sds-2) and [have their own distribution](https://www.researchgate.net/post/Standard_Deviation_Distribution/59032925ed99e1ba910f11ff/citation/download), around the `pop_sd`.[^5]. This distribution of the sample-sds will also have its own `mean` and `sd` too !! Are you confused yet? Hold tight! 😱 😱 😱 😱 ::: [^8]: [^5]: ### {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} {{< iconify tabler chart-histogram >}} Distribution of Sample-Means So now let's plot the **distribution** of these 500 sample-means themselves, called [**a distribution of sample-means**]{.bg-yellow .black}. We will also plot the position of the population mean `pop_mean` parameter, the mean of the `Height` variable. ::: callout-note WHY? Because we want to see how the sample-means are distributed around the population mean, and how they compare with the population distribution itself. ::: ::: {#fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution .cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) sample_50_500 %>% gf_dhistogram(~sample_mean, bins = 30, xlab = "Sample Means only") %>% gf_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, color = "blue" ) %>% gf_label(0.01 ~ pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "blue" ) %>% gf_labs( title = "Sampling Mean Distribution", subtitle = "500 means" ) # How does this **distribution of sample-means** compare with the # overall distribution of the population? # sample_50_500 %>% gf_dhistogram(~sample_mean, bins = 30, xlab = "Sample Means, and the Height variable") %>% gf_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, color = "blue" ) %>% gf_label(0.01 ~ pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "blue" ) %>% ## Add the population histogram gf_histogram(~Height, data = NHANES_adult, alpha = 0.2, fill = "blue", bins = 30 ) %>% gf_label(0.025 ~ (pop_mean + 20), label = "Population Distribution of Height", color = "blue" ) %>% gf_labs( title = "Sampling Mean Distribution", subtitle = "Original Population overlay" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample Means Distribution](index_files/figure-html/fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution-1.png){#fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution-1 width=2100} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample Means Distribution overlaid with Population Distribution](index_files/figure-html/fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution-2.png){#fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution-2 width=2100} ::: Sample Mean Distribution ::: ### {{< iconify carbon concept >}} Deriving the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) We see in the @fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution-1 above that - the *distribution of sample-means* is centered around the `pop_mean`. ( Mean of the sample means = `pop_mean`!! 😱) - That the "spread" aka `sd` of the *distribution of sample means* is within than population itself. [Well within](https://www.alice-in-wonderland.net/resources/chapters-script/alices-adventures-in-wonderland/chapter-7/) ! Curiouser and curiouser! - But exactly how much is it? And what is the kind of distribution? - Why are we interested? *Any single sample* needs to give us a `pop_mean` estimate. And it had better be good, with small standard deviation. - Does the sample ***size*** matter? Does the sample mean distribution change with sample size? One more experiment. Now let's repeatedly sample `Height` and compute the sample-means, and look at the resulting histograms. (We will deal with sample-standard-deviations shortly.) We will also use sample sizes of `c(8, 16, 32, 64)` and generate 1000 samples each time, take the means and plot these 4 * 1000 means: :::: {layout="[25,25, 25, 25]"} ::: {#first-column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(12345) samples_08_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, size = 08 ) %>% mean() samples_08_1000 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Means of 1000 samples of size 8 ::: ::: {#second-column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(12345) samples_16_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, size = 16 ) %>% mean() samples_16_1000 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Means of 1000 samples of size 16 ::: ::: {#third-column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(12345) samples_32_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, size = 32 ) %>% mean() samples_32_1000 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Means of 1000 samples of size 32 ::: ::: {#fourth-column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(12345) samples_64_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, size = 64 ) %>% mean() samples_64_1000 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Means of 1000 samples of size 64 ::: :::: ::: {.cell} ::: Let us plot their individual histograms to compare them: ::: {#fig-sampling-distributions .cell layout-nrow="2" layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) # Let us overlay their individual histograms to compare them: p5 <- gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_08_1000, color = "grey", fill = "dodgerblue", title = "N = 8" ) %>% gf_fitdistr(linewidth = 1) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, inherit = FALSE, color = "blue" ) %>% gf_label(-0.025 ~ pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "blue" ) %>% gf_theme(scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.02)))) ## p6 <- gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_16_1000, color = "grey", fill = "sienna", title = "N = 16" ) %>% gf_fitdistr(linewidth = 1) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, color = "blue" ) %>% gf_label(-.025 ~ pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "blue" ) %>% gf_theme(scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.02)))) ## p7 <- gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_32_1000, na.rm = TRUE, color = "grey", fill = "palegreen", title = "N = 32" ) %>% gf_fitdistr(linewidth = 1) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, color = "blue" ) %>% gf_label(-.025 ~ pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "blue" ) %>% gf_theme(scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.02)))) p8 <- gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_64_1000, na.rm = TRUE, color = "grey", fill = "violetred", title = "N = 64" ) %>% gf_fitdistr(linewidth = 1) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, color = "blue" ) %>% gf_label(-.025 ~ pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "blue" ) %>% gf_theme(scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.02)))) # patchwork::wrap_plots(p5,p6,p7,p8) p5 p6 p7 p8 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample Size = 8](index_files/figure-html/fig-sampling-distributions-1.png){#fig-sampling-distributions-1 width=2100} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample Size = 16](index_files/figure-html/fig-sampling-distributions-2.png){#fig-sampling-distributions-2 width=2100} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample Size = 32](index_files/figure-html/fig-sampling-distributions-3.png){#fig-sampling-distributions-3 width=2100} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample Size = 64](index_files/figure-html/fig-sampling-distributions-4.png){#fig-sampling-distributions-4 width=2100} ::: Sampling Distributions ::: And if we overlay these histograms on top of one another: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_08_1000, color = "grey", fill = "dodgerblue", alpha = .5 ) %>% # gf_label(0.15 ~ 172, inherit = FALSE, # label = "N = 8", color = "dodgerblue") %>% gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_16_1000, color = "grey", fill = "sienna", alpha = 0.5 ) %>% # gf_label(0.2 ~ 172, # label = "N = 16", color = "sienna") %>% gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_32_1000, color = "grey", fill = "palegreen", alpha = 0.5 ) %>% # gf_label(0.3 ~ 172, # label = "N = 32", color = "palegreen") %>% gf_dhistogram(~result, data = samples_64_1000, color = "grey", fill = "violetred", alpha = 0.5 ) %>% # gf_label(0.4 ~ 172, # label = "N = 64", color = "violetred") %>% gf_fitdistr( ~result, data = samples_08_1000, color = "dodgerblue", size = 2 ) %>% gf_fitdistr( ~result, data = samples_16_1000, color = "sienna", size = 2 ) %>% gf_fitdistr( ~result, data = samples_32_1000, na.rm = TRUE, color = "palegreen", size = 2 ) %>% gf_fitdistr( ~result, data = samples_64_1000, na.rm = TRUE, color = "violetred", size = 2 ) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, color = "blue" ) %>% gf_label(-.02 ~ pop_mean, label = "Population Mean", color = "blue" ) %>% gf_annotate( geom = "label", x = 175, y = 0.25, label = "N = 64", colour = "violetred" ) %>% gf_annotate( geom = "label", x = 175, y = 0.2, label = "N = 32", colour = "lightgreen" ) %>% gf_annotate( geom = "label", x = 175, y = 0.15, label = "N = 16", colour = "sienna" ) %>% gf_annotate( geom = "label", x = 175, y = 0.1, label = "N = 8", colour = "dodgerblue" ) %>% gf_annotate("curve", x = 175, y = 0.24, xend = 171, yend = 0.22, curvature = 0, color = "violetred", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")) ) %>% gf_annotate("curve", x = 175, y = 0.19, xend = 171, yend = 0.17, curvature = 0, color = "green", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")) ) %>% gf_annotate("curve", x = 175, y = 0.14, xend = 171, yend = 0.12, curvature = 0, color = "sienna", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")) ) %>% gf_annotate("curve", x = 175, y = 0.09, xend = 172, yend = 0.08, curvature = 0, color = "dodgerblue", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")) ) %>% gf_labs(title = "Overlaid Sample Mean Distributions") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![All Sampling Mean Distributions Overlay](index_files/figure-html/fig-overlaid-distributions-1.png){#fig-overlaid-distributions width=2100} ::: ::: From the histograms we learn that the sample-means are **normally distributed** around the *population mean*. [This feels intuitively right because when we sample from the population, many values will be close to the *population mean*, and values far away from the mean will be increasingly scarce.]{style="background-color: yellow;"} Let us calculate the means of the **sample-mean-distributions**: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(~result, data = samples_08_1000) # Mean of means!!!;-0 mean(~result, data = samples_16_1000) mean(~result, data = samples_32_1000) mean(~result, data = samples_64_1000) pop_mean ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 168.2391 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 168.2224 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 168.3131 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 168.3706 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 168.3497 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: All are nearly identical, and also pretty close to the population mean !!! So regardless of sample size, we get an estimate of the `pop_mean` from the mean of a sample! Whoo-Hoo!!! But how good can the estimate be? How much uncertainty is there in this estimate? For that, we need to look at the *standard deviations* of the sampling distributions: $$ \Large{sd_i = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma[{x_i - \bar{x_i}}]^2}{n_i}}} $$ ::::: columns ::: column We take the sum of all *squared [differences]{.bg-washed-red .black}* from the mean in a sample. If we divide this sum-of-squared-differences by the sample length $n$, we get a sort of *average squared difference*, or *per-capita* squared error from the mean, which is called the **variance**. Taking the square root gives us an average error, which we would call, of course, the *standard deviation*. ::: ::: column ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/showing-variance-calculation-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pop_sd sd(~result, data = samples_08_1000) sd(~result, data = samples_16_1000) sd(~result, data = samples_32_1000) sd(~result, data = samples_64_1000) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.15705 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.70518 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.635219 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.874483 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.333163 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: These are also decreasing steadily with sample size. How are they related to the `pop_sd`? ::::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pop_sd pop_sd / sqrt(8) pop_sd / sqrt(16) pop_sd / sqrt(32) pop_sd / sqrt(64) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.15705 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.591058 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.539262 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.795529 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.269631 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: As we can see, the *standard deviations* of the **sampling-mean-distributions** is inversely proportional to the square root of lengths of the sample. Which means that as we increase the sample size of our planned single sample, the *standard deviation* of the sample-mean-distribution decreases, and so does the uncertainty in our estimate of the `pop_mean`! ::: callout-note ## Central Limit Theorem Now we have enough to state the **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)** - the [sample-means are normally distributed around the *population mean*]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. So any mean of a **single sample** is a good, **unbiased estimate** for the `pop_mean`. - $\Large{\bar{x} \sim pop.mean }$ - the **sample-mean distributions** are centered around the `pop_mean` and have a *standard deviation* that is [inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. - $\Large{s \sim \frac{pop.sd}{sqrt(n)} }$ - This is [regardless of the distribution of the *population*]{style="background-color: yellow;"} itself.[^1] ::: [^1]: The `Height` variable seems to be normally distributed at population level. We will try other non-normal population variables as an exercise in the tutorials. This theorem underlies all our procedures and techniques for statistical inference, as we shall see. {{< video https://youtu.be/_YOr_yYPytM >}} ## {{< iconify dashicons code-standards >}} The Standard Error Consider once again the *standard deviations* in each of the **sample-mean-distributions** that we have generated. As we saw these decrease with sample size. `sd = pop_sd/sqrt(sample_size)`where sample-size[^2] here is one of `c(8, 16, 32, 64)`. [^2]: Once `sample size = population`, we have complete access to the population and there is no question of estimation error! So `sample_sd = pop_sd`! ::: callout-important We reserve the term *Standard Deviation* for the population, and name this computed standard deviation of the sample-mean-distributions as the **Standard Error**. This statistic derived from the sample-mean-distribution will help us infer our population parameters with a precise estimate of the *uncertainty* involved. ::: $$ \Large{Standard\ Error\ \pmb {se} = \frac{pop.sd}{\sqrt[]{n}}}\\ $${#eq-standard-error} [However, we don't normally know the `pop_sd`!! So now what?? So is this chicken and egg??]{style="background-color: yellow;"} ## {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} Back to One Sample!! Let us take **SINGLE SAMPLES** of each size, as we normally would: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(42) sample_08 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 8) sample_16 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 16) sample_32 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 32) sample_64 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 64) ## pop_sd sd(~Height, data = sample_08) sd(~Height, data = sample_16) sd(~Height, data = sample_32) sd(~Height, data = sample_64) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.15705 [1] 11.18261 [1] 9.655411 [1] 12.29982 [1] 9.501044 ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-warning ### Distribution of Sample SDs As we saw at the start of this module, the sample-means are distributed around the `pop_mean`, AND it appears that the sample-sds are also distributed around the `pop_sd`! However, the sample-sd distribution is **not Gaussian** (because an sd can never be negative), and the sample_sd is also **not an unbiased estimate** for the `pop_sd`. However, when the sample size $n$ is large ($n >= 30$), the sample-sd distribution approximates the Gaussian, and the bias is small. ::: And so, in the same way, [we approximate the `pop_sd` with the sd of a **single sample** of the same length]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. Hence the *Standard Error* can be computed from **a single sample** as: $$ \Large{Standard\ Error\ \pmb {se} \sim \frac{sample.sd}{\sqrt[]{n}}} $$ With these, the Standard Errors(SE) evaluate to: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pop_sd sd(~Height, data = sample_08) / sqrt(8) sd(~Height, data = sample_16) / sqrt(16) sd(~Height, data = sample_32) / sqrt(32) sd(~Height, data = sample_64) / sqrt(64) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.15705 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.953649 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.413853 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.174321 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.187631 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: Why are we concerned with Standard Errors(SE)? Because they are the **uncertainty** in our sample-mean estimates of the population mean. And when we want to be **more certain**, we need to reduce the SE and therefore...make our sample larger. Design hack! ## {{< iconify fluent auto-fit-width-24-filled >}} Confidence intervals When we work with samples, we want to be able to speak with a certain degree of confidence about the **population mean**, based on the evaluation of **one** sample mean, not a large number of them. Given that sample-means are *normally distributed* around the `pop_mean`, we can say that: - $68\%$ of *all possible sample-mean* lie within $\pm 1* SE$ of the *population mean*; - $95 \%$ of *all possible sample-mean* lie within $\pm 2 * SE$ of the *population mean*. - These two multiplier-constants $\pm 1$ and $\pm 2$ are the `z-scores` from the *z-distribution* we saw earlier: ::: {#fig-confidence-intervals-examples .cell layout-ncol="3"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(42) mosaic::xqnorm(p = c((1 - 0.68) / 2, 1 - (1 - 0.68) / 2), return = c("plot"), verbose = F) mosaic::xqnorm(p = c((1 - 0.95) / 2, 1 - (1 - 0.95) / 2), return = c("plot"), verbose = F) TeachingDemos::ci.examp(mean.sim = 100, sd = 2, n = 50, reps = 50) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![68% Confidence Intervals](index_files/figure-html/fig-confidence-intervals-examples-1.png){#fig-confidence-intervals-examples-1 width=2100} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![95% Confidence Intervals](index_files/figure-html/fig-confidence-intervals-examples-2.png){#fig-confidence-intervals-examples-2 width=2100} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![95% CI from Multiple Samples](index_files/figure-html/fig-confidence-intervals-examples-3.png){#fig-confidence-intervals-examples-3 width=2100} ::: Confidence Intervals Examples ::: In @fig-confidence-intervals-examples-3, we see that $95\%$ confidence intervals straddle the population mean shown in black, almost always. One sample in 50 has missed it and is shown in pink. For a particular sample with $\bar{x} = 100$, the vertical red lines show the confidence interval derived from *that* sample. ## CI and Sample Size How do these vary with sample size $n$? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) tbl_1 <- get_ci(samples_08_1000, level = 0.95) tbl_2 <- get_ci(samples_16_1000, level = 0.95) tbl_3 <- get_ci(samples_32_1000, level = 0.95) tbl_4 <- get_ci(samples_64_1000, level = 0.95) rbind(tbl_1, tbl_2, tbl_3, tbl_4) %>% rownames_to_column("index") %>% cbind("sample_size" = c(8, 16, 32, 64)) %>% gf_segment(index + index ~ lower_ci + upper_ci, linewidth = 1) %>% gf_vline(xintercept = pop_mean, colour = "blue", linewidth = 2) %>% gf_labs( title = "95% Confidence Intervals for the Mean", subtitle = "Varying samples sizes 8-16-32-64", y = "Sample Size", x = "Mean Ranges" ) %>% gf_refine(scale_y_discrete(labels = c(8, 16, 32, 64))) %>% gf_annotate(geom = "label", x = pop_mean + 1.75, y = 3.5, label = "Population Mean") %>% gf_annotate("curve", x = pop_mean + 1.75, y = 3.25, xend = pop_mean + 0.25, yend = 1.2, curvature = -0.35, color = "blue", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Confidence Intervals for varying sample sizes](index_files/figure-html/fig-confidence-intervals-sample-sizes-1.png){#fig-confidence-intervals-sample-sizes width=2100} ::: ::: ::: callout-important ## Confidence Intervals Shrink! Yes, with sample size! Why is that a good thing? ::: So finally, [we can *pretend* that our sample is also distributed normally (i.e Gaussian)]{style="background-color: yellow;"} and use its `sample_sd` as a substitute for `pop_sd`, plot the `standard errors` **on the sample histogram**, and see where our *believed mean* is. ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) mean_sample_16 <- mean(~Height, data = sample_16) # Single Sample sd_sample_16 <- sd(~Height, data = sample_16) # Single Sample se_sample_16 <- sd_sample_16 / sqrt(16) # Standard Error xqnorm( p = c(0.025, 0.975), mean = mean_sample_16, sd = se_sample_16, return = c("value"), verbose = T, plot = F ) -> xq ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` If X ~ N(170.9812, 2.413853), then ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` P(X <= 166.2502) = 0.025 P(X <= 175.7123) = 0.975 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` P(X > 166.2502) = 0.975 P(X > 175.7123) = 0.025 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} xqnorm( p = c(0.025, 0.975), mean = mean_sample_16, sd = se_sample_16, digits = 3, return = c("plot"), verbose = F, alpha = 0.5, colour = "black" ) %>% gf_refine(scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = c(0, 0.02)))) %>% gf_vline(xintercept = ~pop_mean, colour = "red", linewidth = 1) %>% gf_vline( xintercept = mean(~Height, data = sample_16), colour = "purple", linewidth = 1 ) %>% gf_labs( x = "Sample Value", title = "Confidence Intervals and the Bell Curve. 2.0 * se_sample_16 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 166.1535 ``` ::: ::: Lower Limit of CI ::: ::: {#fifth-column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} mean_sample_16 + 2.0 * se_sample_16 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 175.809 ``` ::: ::: Upper Limit of CI ::: :::: So: - Every sample we could take sets up a Gaussian distribution for the estimate of the `pop_mean`. (Which is `sample_mean` in this case.) - Each sample will have a different `sample_mean`, and therefore the distribution curves, being centred on `sample_mean` would move to the right or to the left. - Each such sample distribution sets up a Confidence Interval. - We expect that 95% of the samples will setup a Confidence Interval that contains the `pop_mean`. ## {{< iconify flat-color-icons workflow >}} CLT Workflow Thus if we want to estimate a *population mean*: - we take one **random** sample from the population of length $n$ - we calculate the mean from the sample `sample-mean` - we calculate the `sample-sd` - we calculate the *Standard Error* as $\frac{sample-sd}{\sqrt[]{n}}$ - we calculate 95% confidence intervals for the *population parameter* based on the formula $CI_{95\%}= sample.mean \pm 2*SE$. - Since Standard Error decreases with sample size, we need to make our sample of adequate size.( $n=30$ seems appropriate in most cases. Why?) - And we do not have to worry about the distribution of the population. It need not be normal/Gaussian/Bell-shaped !! ## {{< iconify flat-color-icons workflow >}} CLT Assumptions - Population Standard Deviation $\sigma$ is known; - Sample is of "decent length" $n >= 30$; - Therefore sample histogram is Gaussian. When these are violated, as with small sample sizes, or with unknown population sds, we need to use the *t-distribution* instead of the *z-distribution* to calculate confidence intervals. The *t-distribution* is a family of distributions that are similar to the Gaussian, but have heavier tails. This leads to slightly wider Confidence Intervals being computed. ## {{< iconify material-symbols interactive-space-outline >}} An interactive Sampling app Here below is an interactive sampling app. Play with the different settings, especially the *distribution in the population* to get a firm grasp on Sampling and the CLT. ## {{< iconify mingcute thought-line >}} Wait, But Why? - We want to take **one sample** from a population and use it to make inferences about population `parameters` - We compute a `statistic` from the sample, i.e. a `mean` - We want to be able to say how accurate it is, i.e. state its `mean` and `standard deviation`, and the `relative probability` of how probable the `statistic` could be - Relative probabilities, means, and standard deviations are only possible to calculate if we have ***many*** means, and therefore, ***many*** samples!! - So we, as [frequentist]{style="background-color:yellow;"} people, ***pretend*** we can take many samples and calculate the `mean of the means` and the `standard deviation of the means` (Now called `standard error`), and the `relative probability` of a the calculated `statistic` - These tell us how the `mean`s are distributed and how accurate the `mean-mean` can be - Since `standard error` uses the (unknown and unknowable) `population sd`, we approximate that by `sample sd` - So $$ \Large{\mu_{pop} \sim \mu_{sample} \pm 2.0 * \sigma_{sample}}$$ ## {{< iconify ooui references-rtl >}} References 1.
